text: Every equals-equals comparison you've written so far in this course has been quietly risky. This lesson explains why, with a famous one-line proof, and shows the tools quantum computing code uses everywhere instead of exact equality.

A Python float has roughly fifteen to seventeen significant decimal digits of precision under the IEEE 754 standard — extremely accurate, but it means two mathematically identical numbers can come out of different computation paths differing in that last digit or two. math dot isclose, np dot isclose, and np dot allclose compare within a tolerance instead of demanding exact equality. And loosening that tolerance too far, say to point two, would call a genuinely broken result close, which is the real danger of tolerances used carelessly.

Point one plus point two prints as point three zero zero zero zero zero zero zero zero zero zero zero zero zero zero four, and checking it against point three with equals-equals returns False. This isn't a Python bug — the identical result shows up in JavaScript, C, and Java, because point one and point two simply can't be represented exactly in binary. math dot isclose correctly returns True, because the gap is about four times ten to the negative seventeen, vastly smaller than the default tolerance.

Recall from Lesson 10 that two measurement probabilities summed to zero point nine nine nine nine nine nine nine nine nine nine nine nine nine eight, not a clean one. That total equals one point zero with equals-equals returns False, but np dot isclose correctly returns True, because the gap is floating-point noise, not a real bug. This is exactly why no real quantum code checks norm equals one point zero directly.

Next lesson's lab puts the conjugate, transpose, at-sign, allclose, and eigenvalue tools from this chapter together, verifying two real gates and computing the eigenvalues of a genuinely complex Hermitian matrix.
